overview: From Damascus, the Umayyad caliphs governed an empire that eventually stretched from the Atlantic to the Indus. Their eastern caliphate lasted from 661 to 750. The imported map shows only a western portion, combines some separately labelled North African communities, and extends its snapshot to 800. It must not be read as a complete or continuously controlled frontier. Palaces, workshops, farms and surviving paperwork reveal a society much wider than the ruling family.

periods.title: The Damascus-based caliphate
periods.summary: Umayyad dynastic rule preceded and ended before the limits of the imported 700 to 800 map snapshot.

items.text: Muawiya established the dynasty in 661, and Damascus became its capital. Hereditary succession gave the caliphate a ruling family, with members competing for power across successive generations. The empire also borrowed administrative experience from earlier Byzantine and Sasanian governments. Conquering a province and collecting its revenue were different kinds of work.

Expansion brought Umayyad armies into Iberia in 711 and far into Central Asia. It also brought limits: repeated campaigns failed to capture Constantinople. Within the empire, tensions included unequal treatment of non-Arab converts to Islam. The history of this powerful state includes both remarkable expansion and conflicts among people living under its rule.

sections.title: Messages carried by money and monuments

items.text: A gold dinar in the British Museum, dated 696 to 697, replaced a ruler’s portrait with lines of Arabic calligraphy. Three lines fill each face, with more writing around the edge. The coin names neither caliph nor mint, but gives a date and religious declarations. Its design made a small piece of money carry an unmistakable public message.

An Ashmolean gold coin dated 712 to 713 bears “بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم”, meaning “In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate”. This Arabic sample is the museum’s transcription of the reverse inscription on thuluth HCR10035, shown in modern type rather than a facsimile of the lettering. At just 14.3 millimetres across, the coin held a surprisingly visible declaration.

The Great Mosque of Damascus was built between 705 and 715 on a site previously occupied by a temple and then a church. Its gold-ground mosaics helped establish a monumental language for the new rulers. Only part of the original decoration survives; later repairs and restorations are also part of the building visitors see today.

sections.title: Water, warmth and getting rid of waste

items.text: Anjar, founded in the early eighth century in today’s Lebanon, stood where major routes crossed. Its main streets divided the rectangular city into four quarters, with sewer collectors beneath the principal axes. Baths were deliberately placed to help wastewater drain away. City planning included the unglamorous task of deciding where used bathwater should go.

At Quseir Amra in today’s Jordan, elite visitors could move through a changing room into warm and hot bathing rooms. Supplying this comfort required a well, tank and water-lifting equipment. Drainage pipes and a cesspool handled the aftermath. The decorated rooms survive alongside evidence of the workers and infrastructure needed to keep a bath functioning.

Look up inside Quseir Amra’s hot room and the ceiling becomes a painted sky: zodiac signs and constellations curve over its dome. Other murals show people, animals and hunting. This was art for a courtly bathing and reception complex, illustrating how decoration could vary between a ruler’s leisure buildings and religious settings.

Qasr al-Hayr al-Gharbi, founded in 727 between Damascus and Palmyra, was more than a residence for relaxation. Its estate included a dam, lake, mill and irrigated fields, as well as a bath and caravanserai for travellers. Food production, water management and movement along caravan routes helped support the impressive buildings.

At Nahal Anava near Modi’in, excavators distinguished an earlier Byzantine agricultural estate from a later Umayyad farmhouse. A cave containing an olive press had collapsed before the later farmhouse phase, dated between the seventh and mid-eighth centuries. Pottery helped establish the sequence. A farm’s history could involve rebuilding after damage rather than starting afresh when rulers changed.

A letter written in Greek on 30 January 710 ordered Basilius, a local administrator at Aphrodito in Egypt, to supply a boat. It was to carry sailors, workmen and supplies requisitioned for a military expedition. British Library Papyrus 1348 preserves the order. For ordinary workers, imperial warfare could mean transport duties and time away from their usual work.

A child’s linen tunic from Durunkah in Egypt has decorative shoulder bands woven in dark brown thread. National Museums Scotland dates it broadly to the seventh or eighth century, overlapping Umayyad rule without tying it to one reign. This small garment brings clothing-making and a child’s everyday needs into a history often dominated by rulers and battles.

ending.text: The Abbasid overthrow in 750 ended the Damascus-based Umayyad caliphate. Its inhabitants, working landscapes and craft traditions did not disappear with the dynasty. A surviving Umayyad branch later established rule in al-Andalus, a separate political story covered by the Córdoba cards. The imported endpoint of 800 is therefore not the date this eastern caliphate fell.
